**GRID GUARDIAN**

The Decision and Orchestration Layer Between Hazard Detection and Grid Action

MGMT 241 · Technology Innovation · Group 1 · August 23, 2026

# **1\. Executive Summary and Problem Definition**

Grid Guardian helps utility operators make and execute better grid reconfiguration decisions during wildfire emergencies. When a wildfire moves through a service territory, it continuously re-plans how power is distributed, presents each plan to a human operator for approval, executes the approved plan across the utility’s existing switching hardware/notification systems and logs what happened so the next decision is better. It is software. It does not detect fires or model fire spread but  it turns existing hazard, grid and operational data into actionable decisions about how to keep the grid functioning during an emergency. It operates on the decision and orchestration layer between hazard detection and grid action.

The status quo is that every wildfire season, a utility grid operator faces the same decision under time pressure. The decisions are which circuits get de-energized, in what order, and what is being given up to keep a hospital or an evacuation route alive. The decision has to be made in minutes, with incomplete information and potentially severe consequences in either direction. Shut off too much power and critical services and communities are unnecessarily disrupted, but shut off too little and energized infrastructure may increase wildfire risk.

Both directions of decision-making have been documented and expensive. Between 2013 and 2020, Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) shutoff outages cost California utilities and ratepayers an estimated $5.3 billion. PG\&E alone recorded $102 million in de-energization and readiness costs in 2021\. In the other direction of shutting off too little, Hawaiian Electric had to settle a $4 billion lawsuit after a 2023 Maui wildfire due to failure to de-energize after warnings from emergency managers. Hawaiian Electric had no operational wildfire risk model at the time and committed to building one after. PacifiCorp also faced lawsuits for more than $8 billion for Oregon wildfires in 2020\.

Over-shutoff is now drawing regulatory attention of its own. Southern California Edison de-energized roughly 534,000 customers in 2025 against 137,000 the year before, took more than 10,000 critical facilities offline including hospitals, and left some customers without power for as long as fifteen days. The CPUC citation that followed (WSEB-1, W.25-12-001, December 2025\) assessed $7,865,360 across 29 violation categories. That citation focused on how the shutoffs were carried out, particularly failures in customer notification and documentation, not on whether SCE should have de-energized the grid in the first place. There was no regulatory finding criticizing the utility for failing to shut off enough power. The industry challenge, however, is not determining which type of error is worse. Utilities face significant consequences from both unnecessary shutoffs and failing to de-energize when conditions warrant it. Yet they currently lack a comprehensive tool that systematically weighs those competing risks when making real-time decisions. That is where Grid Guardian comes in.

It should be noted that sophisticated wildfire analytics and grid-management tools already exist, particularly among large investor-owned utilities (IOUs) but they solve different pieces of the decision and remain out of reach for many smaller utilities. Grid Guardian fills the gap by providing municipal utilities, cooperatives, and smaller IOUs access to decision-support capabilities they largely do not have today. It is essentially access and orchestration at an operator’s fingertips. The opportunity is therefore not to replace existing wildfire or grid-management technology but to connect it into an actionable decision layer for an underserved market.

In addition, Grid Guardian pursues a path of innovation by solving different sets of decision making. The incumbent yardstick is customer-minutes of outage. Grid Guardian optimizes for something different: emergency response capability during the event, meaning whether people can still evacuate and whether emergency crews can still operate while the fire is active. When power fails during an evacuation, traffic signals go dark, intersections gridlock, evacuation routes clog and crews cannot move. That is a second hazard stacked on the first. The LA County After-Action Review of the Eaton fire records that public safety shutoffs and fire damage to power lines in the Altadena and Pasadena areas “took out streetlights and ambient lighting.” No source establishes that power loss caused deaths and this report does not claim it. The supportable statement is narrower and still decisive: that power loss degraded the conditions under which a mass evacuation took place. Optimizing for civil function rather than number of customer-minutes of outage  is the disruption, and it is what makes the product a decision system rather than a dashboard.

# **2\. Market Opportunity**

Grid Guardian’s addressable market is not the wildfire-risk-analytics or advanced distribution management system (ADMS) categories in the broad sense. Both are dominated by vendors already contracted with the roughly 200 U.S. investor-owned utilities that can afford enterprise-scale tools: Technosylva in risk analytics, and GE Vernova, Schneider Electric and Oracle Utilities in grid management.

The market opportunity is the segment those incumbents structurally cannot serve: the more than 2,770 non-IOU electric utilities in the U.S. comprising 1,958 publicly owned utilities and 812 electric cooperatives, plus the county and state emergency management agencies that coordinate alongside them.

**Sizing, from the bottom up.** Non-IOU utilities represent roughly $156 billion in aggregate annual operating revenue. At a 5% software-spend benchmark, that implies a TAM of approximately $7.8 billion. For scale, the entire ADMS software market is estimated between $2.1 billion and $3.8 billion depending on the source, which is itself a reason to treat any single published market figure with caution. The SAM is the wildfire- and weather-exposed subset carrying an active mitigation-planning obligation. Using the share of U.S. housing in the wildland-urban interface, roughly 32%, as the proxy for that subset gives a SAM of approximately $2.5 billion.

The serviceable obtainable market is deliberately modest, because it is bounded by the sales cycle rather than by demand. Fire season forces a single annual onboarding window of January through May, and a first municipal or cooperative customer takes seven to twelve months to close. The base case therefore reaches approximately 105 customers and $12.2 million of annual recurring revenue in Year 5\. That is about 3.8% of the non-IOU utility base by customer count and roughly 0.5% of the SAM by revenue, weighted toward the smaller tiers.

**Pricing is calibrated to the segment, not to the top of the market.** Grid Guardian is priced in three tiers: $62,500 per year for municipal utilities and small cooperatives, $186,250 for mid-sized utilities and regional agencies, and $562,500 for large cooperatives and multi-agency contracts. The anchor for the Basic tier is empirical rather than assumed. PG\&E’s disclosed 2021 spend on Technosylva fire-spread modeling was $3.934 million (CPUC filing A.22-12-009); this lands near the Basic tier once scaled down proportionally to the operating revenue of an average municipal or cooperative utility. The pricing reflects what this segment can plausibly pay, not what the top of the market pays.

Grid Guardian is not chasing the large-IOU contracts that Technosylva and EMBERPOINT already hold and should not be modeled as though it were. The defensible claim is narrower and more durable: to be the first real decision-support option for a 2,770-utility segment currently running on spreadsheets and judgment.

# **3\. Product and Technology**

**What the product does, and where it sits.** Grid Guardian's performance is measured by how effectively it helps a utility make better operating decisions during an active wildfire, not by how accurately it predicts or detects the fire. Technosylva, EMBERPOINT, NIFC/IRWIN and satellite sources already supply hazard detection and fire-spread forecasting, and Grid Guardian uses those forecasts as inputs. Grid Guardian’s role begins once a hazard is identified: it evaluates the forecast against current grid conditions and determines how power can be rerouted or selectively de-energized while preserving critical facilities, evacuation corridors and overall emergency response capability.

Existing wildfire analytics set a real benchmark. PG\&E, which uses Technosylva, has reported a 99% reduction in acres impacted by utility-caused wildfires in high fire-threat districts against its 2018-2020 average, alongside a 56% reduction in average PSPS duration. Those results come from a broad mitigation program of which risk analytics is one component, and Grid Guardian is not competing for them. Its performance depends on a different question: whether it can take existing hazard information and produce a feasible operating plan that preserves more critical function without increasing exposure on high-risk circuits. This makes the product complementary to systems utilities already run rather than a replacement for them.

**The five-step loop.** The architecture is a continuous loop, and each step maps to a distinct engine module. Step one ingests the hazard perimeter and forecast track, weather, grid topology and live state, critical facilities and evacuation corridors, crew positions, and a human situational feed, while incorporating utility-defined operating parameters and priorities that establish the boundaries within which recommendations are generated. Step two scores the threat against the affected network and produces a switching plan that keeps the most weighted critical function energized, given which circuits the forecast perimeter will sever, re-solving whenever conditions change materially. Step three presents that plan to a human operator with its scope, customer impact, and critical-facility impact; the operator accepts, narrows, or overrides, and nothing executes without that approval. Step four fans the approved plan out into switch commands for remotely operable devices, crew dispatch for manual ones, customer notification lists, de-energization orders, and a drafted regulatory report. Step five logs predicted against actual outcomes and computes a resilience score that improves across events. Exhibit C shows the full data-to-decision-to-action architecture.

**Which part is the model, and which part is code.** There are three distinct layers and collapsing any two would be an architecture error. The decision layer is generative: the model receives a bounded context packet and proposes a switch plan through structured tool use, never parsed prose. The orchestrator is agentic; it runs the loop, holds the tools, and decides what to do rather than what is true. The constraint checker is deterministic code with no AI in it, a pure function the orchestrator calls as a tool to prove a plan is electrically valid. Cycle detection, source reachability and load summation are solved graph problems with exact answers, and a model performing them would be slower, non-reproducible and less accurate than a few lines of code. The intelligence belongs in deciding what to do with the verdict, not in producing it.

The judgment calls that make this genuinely agentic are the ones with no closed-form answer: whether a change warrants a re-plan, which of two conflicting feeds to trust when a field report contradicts a sensor, whether a validation failure should be repaired or escalated, how to sequence a fan-out in which some devices switch in seconds and others need a truck, how to allocate scarce line crews across two simultaneous fires, and when to stop and ask a human. The model reasons over a hazard-local subgraph of roughly 30 to 50 assets plus its tie neighbors, never the whole network, which bounds both latency and inference cost and mirrors how an operator actually works. After two failed attempts or an API timeout, a deterministic fallback solver runs and the interface labels the plan as fallback.

**Data requirements are an integration problem, not an acquisition problem.** Grid topology and asset data come from the utility's own GIS, live conditions from SCADA or ADMS, and additional telemetry from AMI. Hazard data comes from third-party providers the utility often already licenses, and weather from the National Weather Service, RAWS and utility-owned stations. Critical facility inventories are public. Almost every input is therefore public, already licensed by the customer, or the customer's own data, which means there is no recurring data-licensing cost and the deployment cost is engineering time that falls with each connector reused. Grid Guardian requires read access to GIS, SCADA state, AMI and workforce location, all standard integrations utilities perform routinely for outage-management vendors, plus write access to switching gated behind the human approval step.

Performance also depends on how much distribution automation a utility already has. Remotely operable switches let an approved action execute in seconds; manual switches require a crew roll, with confirmed timings of roughly ten minutes to assess an event and five minutes per load transfer. Grid Guardian operates with whatever switching granularity a utility has today and produces more surgical plans as automation intensity rises, and it quantifies the outage cost of each missing remote switch as an input to the utility's own capital planning. For manual devices it also supports crew pre-positioning, identifying where crews need to be and how far ahead of the projected hazard they must arrive, which matters most for the municipal and cooperative utilities that have fewer crews and less automation.

# **4\. What the Prototype Demonstrates**

The team built a working prototype using AI-assisted development. It is a Next.js operator console rendering a MapLibre grid map over real Los Angeles basin geography, with a deterministic simulation engine, a nine-rule constraint validator, an impact module and a fallback solver, all exercised by test harnesses that fail the build rather than warn. Forty-four measured values are pinned and compared on every run.

**The claim is structural, not predictive.** A predictive claim, meaning what would happen at a real utility, requires a model calibrated to that utility. This is not one and is never presented as one. The structural claim is that optimizing for civil function and optimizing for customer count produce different plans over the same network, and that requires only that the model be structurally correct: a radial distribution layer at the measured average feeder graph degree of 1.9 to 2.06 observed across 5,020 real U.S. feeders, a meshed upper grid, sparse ties, and critical function unevenly distributed. All four are calibrated to published structure and none depends on the fire being realistic.

The headline finding is a mechanism rather than a magnitude. Counting customers and counting civil function are not the same measurement: in the modelled territory, 1,209 facility nodes hold 10.41 percent of customers but 55.30 percent of weighted civil function. A tool optimizing customer-minutes of outage is therefore not optimizing for whether a city can evacuate. The prototype demonstrates that the two objectives generate different plans over identical inputs, which is precisely the gap the product exists to fill.

**What the prototype does not establish.** The 12 kV distribution network is synthetic, because real feeder-level topology is classified as Critical Energy Infrastructure Information and is not public; it is generated over real transmission corridor geometry published by the California Energy Commission under CC-BY, and every generated asset is marked synthetic in the interface. Service territory, population, employment, terrain and critical-facility coordinates are real. The fire is an input generator rather than a fire model, with no ember spotting, no merge acceleration and no suppression. There is no voltage or impedance representation anywhere, so transfers are screened on thermal capacity and topology alone and a reroute is never described as electrically verified. Results were measured across three ignition events, which is the entire sample; the facility weights are the team's own judgment and are presented as assumptions rather than facts. The prototype cannot and does not claim predictive accuracy against any real utility outcome.

# **5\. Model Currency and Threat Evolution**

Grid Guardian has to stay useful in an environment where wildfire conditions keep changing. Historical patterns are becoming less reliable as extreme heat, drought, vegetation stress, fuel moisture and wind behavior shift, and a decision system built only on historical relationships would degrade even if its technology never changed.

**The division of labor is what makes this tractable.** Grid Guardian stays current by separating changing conditions from fixed electrical rules. It relies on external hazard and weather providers for updated forecasts and re-evaluates its operating recommendations whenever conditions materially change. Meanwhile, electrical constraints such as connectivity and capacity are validated through deterministic code rather than relearned by the AI.

**The compounding asset is the decision-outcome log.** Each event produces a record: the conditions faced, the plan proposed, the validator's verdict, what the operator decided, what was executed, and what followed. Operator overrides are the highest-value rows, because an override is a labelled human correction of exactly the shape that supervised fine-tuning consumes, and it is generated as a by-product of an approval step that exists for liability reasons anyway. The liability answer and the moat are the same mechanism. Over time these decision-outcome pairs become the basis for fine-tuning and improved orchestration policy grounded in real utility decisions rather than in simulation.

One clarification matters for accuracy. Grid Guardian does not train or fine-tune a model today. The accurate description of current practice is in-context grounding on historical event data, with fine-tuning on accumulated decision-outcome pairs as the production path. Any claim that the product trains a model on customer data today would be false.

**The limit on the flywheel, stated plainly.** Utility grid topology can constitute Critical Energy Infrastructure Information, and customer confidentiality may restrict how much raw operating data can be combined across utilities. The moat therefore cannot depend on unrestricted pooling of customer data. A production deployment will likely need to learn from derived or non-identifying characteristics while sensitive topology stays inside each utility's environment. How much of the learning advantage compounds across customers rather than within a single customer is an open question, and resolving it determines how strong the moat actually becomes.

# **6\. Competitive Landscape and Sustainable Advantage**

Every player in the wildfire and grid-resilience space optimizes something different, and that difference, rather than feature parity, is the right axis for competitive analysis. Almost all of them resolve, directly or indirectly, to the same yardstick: customer-minutes of outage. In contrast, Grid Guardian optimizes emergency response capability during the event, and it is the only participant that logs decision outcomes in order to improve the next decision. Exhibit B compares the field on both axes.

**The landscape.** Wildfire risk analytics, principally Technosylva and the analytics layer of EMBERPOINT, is the nearest neighbor. Hazard detection, including EMBERPOINT's sensing layer, optimizes detection latency and feeds our decision layer as an input rather than producing a decision. ADMS and outage management systems from GE Vernova, Schneider Electric, Oracle Utilities, Survalent and Milsoft execute switching and restore service after a fault, but carry no forward-looking view of an active hazard; Grid Guardian sits beside them, not in place of them. Distribution automation manufacturers such as S\&C, G\&W, Eaton and SEL sell the switches our plans operate and are channel partners rather than competitors. Vegetation and asset analytics score ignition probability before an event and become irrelevant once one is underway. Evacuation and public alerting platforms move and inform people but never touch the grid. None of these objective functions is emergency response capability during an active event, and none closes the loop on decision outcomes.

**The real incumbent is a spreadsheet.** The status quo is a wildfire mitigation plan, a fire potential index, per-circuit wind thresholds and operator judgment under time pressure. It is the hardest competitor to displace because it costs nothing incremental, it is already regulator-approved, and no one is criticized for using it. Its weakness is structural: a spreadsheet cannot re-plan continuously against a moving perimeter, it cannot evaluate backfeed options across dozens of ties inside the decision window, and it produces no record that makes the next call better. Under time pressure its safe-looking choice is always to de-energize more than necessary, which is how the over-shutoff pattern regulators are now scrutinizing gets produced in the first place.

**The sharpest contrast.** Technosylva is strong, well-funded and embedded at the largest IOUs, and both products operate in real time during an active event. The difference is what each optimizes. Technosylva recommends whether and where to de-energize, scored against wildfire consequence versus the public-safety cost of shutting off power. Grid Guardian recommends how to reconfigure the grid to keep specific loads energized, scored against emergency response capability. A customer-minutes metric does not distinguish an evacuation-route signal from a single household, and our critical-facility weighting and evacuation-corridor continuity logic exist precisely to break that equivalence. This is not a head-to-head: their perimeter forecast is an input to our decision layer, not a substitute for it, and a joint deployment is coherent and should be the default framing in customer conversations.

**The sustainable advantage, ranked honestly.** First, the decision-outcome log: this is the only genuinely compounding asset, which exists because we log against a different metric than everyone else and which a later entrant cannot buy. Second, the weighted function-lost model: the facility inventory beneath it is public data, but the weighting logic and evacuation-corridor continuity model are ours and are what make the objective function different. Third, the orchestration policy: it is copyable in principle, though the flywheel that improves it is not. Everything else in the stack is the customer's own data, a public feed, or a commodity input licensed from a third party. A synthesis layer claiming to own its inputs would be claiming to be four companies it is not, and each of those companies is better at its own layer than we would be.

**Competitive risks.** An ADMS vendor could bundle a free wildfire module; this is mitigated partly by the outcome log and partly by reaching municipal and cooperative buyers those vendors underserve. A wildfire analytics vendor could add switching recommendations with its own weighting and validation. And utilities may simply stay with the status quo, because an established practice is already defensible in a prudency review while deviating from it would shift liability onto whoever approved the change.

# **7\. Go-to-Market and Customer Adoption**

**The beachhead.** Grid Guardian sells first to municipal utilities and electric cooperatives in high fire-threat territory, with small and mid-sized IOUs such as Liberty Utilities CalPeco and Bear Valley Electric in the same Phase 1 motion. Exhibit D maps the full landscape. The logic is not only price. These utilities typically own distribution and subtransmission but no transmission, so a switching plan routes to one internal approver rather than across an ownership boundary. They also frequently operate the traffic signals and the emergency operations center in the same jurisdiction as the grid, which makes the civil-function objective an internal budget argument rather than an externality they cannot capture. Large IOUs are a Phase 2 upsell, sold as a synthesis layer above the Technosylva and ADMS deployments they already run.

**The regulatory hook is not the CPUC.** The California Public Utilities Commission and the Office of Energy Infrastructure Safety review IOU wildfire mitigation plans, but the beachhead is not CPUC-jurisdictional. Under SB 901 and AB 1054, every California publicly owned utility and electrical cooperative must prepare a Wildfire Mitigation Plan annually, contract a qualified independent evaluator to assess its comprehensiveness, present it to its own governing board, and submit it to the California Wildfire Safety Advisory Board by July 1 each year. That is the better hook: annual rather than multi-year, approved by the buyer's own board rather than a state regulator, and carrying an independent-evaluator requirement that the decision-outcome log is built to satisfy.

**One clock, not two.** That filing deadline and fire season resolve into a single annual rhythm that governs both the go-to-market plan and the revenue model. Fire season runs roughly June through December and peaks September through December, and no utility will cut over a safety-critical de-energization tool mid-season. Onboarding therefore has to land between January and May, the same months the utility is drafting the plan it files on July 1\. The motion follows: engage in autumn while the season's pain is live, close and onboard January through May, and let the customer name Grid Guardian as a mitigation measure in that filing. Miss the window and the prospect waits a year, which is why customer acquisition is modelled as an annual batch rather than a smooth monthly ramp.

**Drill mode answers the off-season.** That gate would otherwise leave seven dead months a year. It does not, because scenario playback becomes drill and exercise mode against the customer's real topology, which is training utilities and county emergency management already run and already budgeted for. At $10,000 per event or $20,000 annually, it is a low-friction paid entry point during fire season itself, when a cutover is impossible but urgency is highest, and it generates operator-override records that seed the decision-outcome log before a live event ever runs. Drill mode is the land; the subscription is the expand.

**Land and expand into SLED.** County and state emergency management agencies cannot execute de-energization and are not the first paying customer. They are already a built product surface, though: the read-only agency view filters by jurisdiction rather than by circuit, which is how a county emergency manager thinks. The efficient motion attaches the agency at $40,000 per year to a utility already deployed in the same county rather than selling cold into a grant cycle.

**Select design partners for connector reuse.** Deployment cost falls from roughly $500,000 to $175,000 as connectors are reused, which is the largest single lever on both gross margin and cycle length. That makes the criterion for the first two or three design partners concrete: choose utilities running the same GIS and ADMS stack as each other. Esri ArcGIS Utility Network is the dominant schema, with CYME, Synergi and Milsoft the common planning models. Two customers on one stack are worth more than two on two stacks, and Milsoft is worth targeting first because its installed base skews toward the cooperative and municipal segment we are entering.

**Channel comes second, deliberately.** NRECA, APPA and the state municipal-utility associations are the efficient route into a fragmented long tail, but they generally want a reference customer before endorsing a vendor, which makes them a Phase 2 scaling motion rather than a Day 1 channel. The nearer-term partnership is with the distribution automation manufacturers: our switch-placement recommendation quantifies the outage cost of every missing remote switch, which sells their hardware. It is a $50,000 SKU and a referral relationship at the same time, with a partner whose incentives point the same direction as ours.

# **8\. Stakeholder Analysis and Risks**

**Who benefits.** Utilities are the primary customers and direct beneficiaries. Municipal utilities, cooperatives and small to mid-sized IOUs gain a decision-support capability for responding to a moving wildfire while balancing two competing risks: leaving threatened infrastructure energized too long, and de-energizing more of the system than necessary. Ratepayers and communities benefit when a utility can determine more precisely what must be de-energized while preserving critical civil functions. Hospitals, emergency operations centers, fire stations and evacuation corridors do not carry the same societal consequences as an individual residential load, yet conventional outage metrics do not distinguish between them. State and local emergency management agencies gain visibility into how a utility's decisions affect the communities they coordinate for. Insurers may eventually benefit from the decision-outcome data as evidence about operational risk. None of these stakeholders needs to become a paying customer for the product to create value for them.

**Operators are the pivotal stakeholder, and the pivotal risk.** Grid operators are ultimately responsible for evaluating and approving recommendations, which makes them both the adoption gate and a potential source of resistance. They may value having hazard, grid, facility and crew information synthesized into a recommended course of action under time pressure, particularly during simultaneous events. They may equally resist a system they perceive as displacing professional judgment or adding complexity during an emergency. The human-in-the-loop architecture addresses this directly: operators accept, narrow, or override, and nothing executes without approval. Those overrides also become the highest-value training records, so human oversight is not merely an adoption accommodation but integral to both the risk controls and the long-term data advantage.

**Who is harmed, and who will object.** The same decisions that create benefit can create harm. An overly cautious recommendation could unnecessarily de-energize customers, disrupt businesses and affect vulnerable communities. A recommendation that leaves threatened infrastructure energized could increase exposure. This creates real liability and regulatory concern, particularly because adopting an AI-supported recommendation may be harder to defend than following an established process that has already survived regulatory review. Grid Guardian cannot eliminate that tension; it can only make the process more transparent and auditable through deterministic validation, documented recommendations, human approval and outcome logging. The critical-facility weights are the sharpest ethical exposure. Deciding what a traffic signal is worth relative to a hospital is a policy judgment, not a technical fact, and if some communities repeatedly experience greater disruption than others, then the objection is legitimate. The honest response is to expose the weights and make them configurable by the utility and its regulator rather than to bury them in a model with the final decision made by a human.

**Technical risk.** The prototype demonstrates a decision framework, not accuracy against a real utility. Its 12 kV network is synthetic, its wildfire forecast is generated rather than supplied by a production hazard provider, and the electrical model represents neither voltage, impedance, protection coordination nor phase balance. A plan that passes the prototype's topology and thermal checks could still prove infeasible on a real network. Recommendation quality also depends entirely on input quality: a real hazard forecast can be wrong, and a wrong forecast produces action against the wrong assets. These limitations make conservative deployment, real utility pilots, deterministic validation and continued human authority necessary before the system could be trusted in live operations.

**Competitive and market risk.** Grid Guardian is not entering an open market. Technosylva, EMBERPOINT, the major ADMS and OMS providers, and the distribution-automation companies all hold significant capability, funding, and customer relationships, and the status quo may be the most difficult competitor of all. Incumbents could extend into the decision layer or bundle comparable capability into platforms utilities already own. The opportunity therefore does not rest on claiming better detection or better fire-spread modeling, which would be false. It rests on proving that a different objective, preserving emergency response capability during an active event, plus orchestration and outcome logging, creates enough incremental value to justify adoption alongside systems already in place.

# **9\. Financials and the Ask**

**Pricing.** Grid Guardian uses a tiered per-site subscription: Basic at $62,500 per year for municipal utilities and small cooperatives, Pro at $186,250 for mid-sized utilities and regional agencies, and Enterprise at $562,500 for large cooperatives and multi-agency contracts. Internal costs scale with model calls, meaning events, and material changes, rather than with customer count. Three add-on SKUs complement the base subscription: the SLED coordination view at $40,000 per year, drill and exercise mode at $10,000 per event or $20,000 annually, and the switch-placement recommendation at $50,000.

**The revenue ramp is bounded by the onboarding window, not by demand.** Because fire season permits a single January-to-May onboarding window and a first municipal customer takes seven to twelve months to close, Year 1 is deliberately modelled at three design partners rather than a continuous ramp. Growth compounds from Year 2 as connectors are reused and reference customers unlock the association channel. Exhibit A carries the full model.

The base case reaches approximately 105 customers and $12.2 million of ARR in Year 5, which is roughly 3.8 percent of the 2,770-utility non-IOU base by count and about 0.5 percent of the $2.6 billion SAM by revenue. Cumulative five-year revenue is approximately $24 million.

**Unit economics.** Gross margin is modelled at 80 percent, consistent with enterprise B2B SaaS benchmarks of 75 to 85 percent, and helped materially by the absence of any recurring data-licensing cost: almost every input is public, customer-owned, or already licensed by the customer. Weighted average ACV across the Year 5 customer mix is approximately $116,000, rising toward $130,000 where add-ons attach. Customer acquisition cost is modelled at $25,000, covering sales effort, pilot customization, and compliance support, which supports a payback period of roughly twelve months at the Basic tier and shorter at higher tiers. Inference cost is bounded by design rather than by hope: subgraph scoping to 30 to 50 assets and a material-change invocation policy hold model spend near $7,500 per month at scale. Deployment cost falls from roughly $500,000 for a first-of-stack integration to about $175,000 as connectors are reused, which is the single largest driver of both margin and cycle time.

**The ask.** Grid Guardian is raising a $2.5 million seed for an 18-month runway, to carry the prototype through to two or three paying design partners, build the production connectors, and convert drill-mode engagements into subscriptions. A $10 million Series A follows on a 24-month runway to scale the commercial team, extend beyond wildfire into flood and wind scenarios, and build out the multi-tenant learning architecture that the CEII constraint requires. Non-dilutive funding is a burn-reduction instrument rather than an acceleration one: SBIR programmes at the Department of Energy, the National Science Foundation or DHS/FEMA, targeted at $1 million to $2 million, run on 6 to 12-month award cycles and will not shorten a customer's procurement, and pilot cost-sharing with early utility and agency customers offsets part of the deployment cost. Total capitalization of $12.5 million to $13.5 million is modelled to reach cash-flow positivity.

**The honest sensitivity.** The model's dominant risk is not price or churn but timing. Because acquisition is gated to one window a year, a single missed pre-season window pushes a cohort a full twelve months and compresses the runway more than any plausible pricing error. That is the number to stress-test first, and it is the reason drill mode exists as an in-season revenue path.

# **10\. Recommended Actions**

Four recommendations follow from the analysis above, in the order they should be executed.

**One: complete the generative decision layer before the next pre-season window.** The validator, impact module, and fallback solver are built and harness-tested; the context packet and model call are the remaining functional work. That sequence was deliberate, because it means every debugging pass runs without spending API calls and a failed API degrades a demo to a labeled fallback rather than ending it. It must nonetheless be finished before a customer-facing pilot.

**Two: sign two to three design partners on a shared GIS and ADMS stack, in one geography.** Stack concentration is worth more than logo diversity at this stage, because connector reuse is what turns a $500,000 integration into a $175,000 one and a twelve-month cycle into a five-month one. A single county with an adjacent emergency management agency also creates the natural SLED attack.

**Three: sell into the Wildfire Mitigation Plan cycle, not around it.** The July 1 filing is the only recurring, board-approved, compliance-driven budget event this segment has. Engage in autumn, onboard January through May, and give the customer something to name in the filing. Use drill mode to hold the relationship and generate outcome data through the months when a cutover is impossible.

**Four: publish the facility weights.** The weighting logic is simultaneously the second-most defensible asset and the largest ethical exposure. Making the weights visible and configurable by the utility and its regulator converts the most credible objection to the product, that a private company is deciding whose power stays on, into a procurement feature. Burying them invites exactly the equity challenge that would stall adoption in the communities most exposed to wildfire.

The disruption Grid Guardian proposes is not a better fire model. It is a change in what the industry optimizes for during an emergency, from customer-minutes of outage to whether a city can still function while it burns. That is a small change in the objective function and a large change in the resulting plan, and it is available to the 2,770 utilities the incumbents were never built to serve.

| **Owns grid switching / topology?** | Yes — full distribution ownership; reconfigure/isolate is directly actionable | Yes, at smaller scale | No — cannot execute de-energization; coordinates and communicates only |
